newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK stocks hit record high, other markets also up.
newsitem.headline: HK stocks hit record high, other markets also up.

text.p: Hong Kong stocks stormed to record highs on Wednesday, as banking and property stocks shot up on expectations of a slew of warrant issues and U.S. economic data soothed interest rate jitters.
The blue chip index posted its third-biggest point gain ever, surging 472.78 points, or 3.56 percent, to a record close of 13,766.65. It hit an intra-day record high of 13,771.54.
Most other Asian bourses also ended higher. Shares in Bangkok climbed by 2.63 percent while those in Seoul rose 1.92 percent despite labour strife.
The Tokyo Stock Exchange was closed for a holiday, gaining a breather from its recent volatility.

Banking and property stocks led the way in Hong Kong, lifted by anticipation that a number of top firms would issue covered warrants. The interest-rate sensitive sectors were also emboldened by developments in the United States.

U.S. bonds benefitted on Tuesday from a benign U.S. December consumer price report that eased fears of an interest-rate hike. The data also pushed the key Dow Jones Industrials stock index to its fourth straight record close.
Hong Kong property stocks also gained on news of high prices paid for two sites at the government's first land auction of 1997, analysts said.
"I think there is every chance 14,500 will be seen in the first quarter," said Miles Remington, sales trader at SocGen-Crosby Securities.
Bangkok stocks took wing after a pledge by Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh to solve the nation's deep economic problems.
Chavalit urged Thais to tighten their belts and vowed that his six-week old government would speed up the slowing economy and narrow the current account deficit.
Brokers said foreign investors seemed most heartened by the promise, and were the most active traders on the day.
The SET index, which declined in the three past consecutive trading days, rose 21.24 points or 2.63 percent to 828.91.
Seoul shares also closed sharply higher with sentiment was buoyed by signs that strikes were fizzling out, brokers said.
Despite all-out strike calls by the nation's two main union umbrella bodies, Seoul was largely unaffected on Wednesday.
The composite index, which briefly sank into negative territory due to profit-taking, ended at a provisional 699.76, up 1.92 percent or 13.17 points.

Expectations that the U.S. market was due for a sharp retreat this year have sparked speculation that foreign funds will turn towards South Korean and other Asian markets, adding to the bullish sentiment, brokers said.
The Australian share market stormed to a record close on the the back of the Dow's strong close.
The All Ordinaries index set sail higher right from the opening bell and closed up 18.8 points or 0.78 percent at 2,438.2, surpassing the previous record close of 2424.6, set on December 31.
"A stronger Dow and a stronger bond market had us looking good for the day," said a Melbourne broker.
Singapore shares bounced off their day's low to end in positive territory. The benchmark Straits Times Industrials Index ended 5.63 points up at 2,221.15 after dropping to a low of 2,212.11.
Key Malaysian blue chips rebounded in the afternoon but failed to lift overall market sentiment.
Traders said interest remained keyed on second line stocks of the main board.

Profit-taking in recent days has dried up, but the market is likely to move sideways in the near term, traders said. The Composite Index of 100 large-capitalised stocks ended up 5.60 points or 0.46 percent to 1,216.64. Crude oil futures prices rose in Singapore. February Brent was last traded at $23.50 per barrel, up 14 cents from London's Tuesday close. March gained 12 cents to $23.10.
Hong Kong gold fell to US$353.00/50 an ounce, down from New York's US$353.70/354.20 close on Monday.
The dollar was firm against the mark and yen, buoyed by speculation by a Bundesbank council member on possible mark weakness. At 1115 GMT, the greenback was at 117.33/7.38 yen and 1.5962/67 marks.
